Vanguard summit: Experts demand action on Mental Health Act, school counselling, affordable care
items.description: •Say Nigeria can’t afford to fail its youth By Sola Ogundipe & Chioma Obinna Nigeria cannot afford to fail its young people as experts at the 4th Vanguard Mental Health Summit called for urgent, coordinated action to address the country’s youth mental health challenges, insisting that government policies, school-based interventions, affordable treatment and stronger accountability must translate into measurable results. Read Also: 2027: 30 days can’t erase over three years of hardship, Atiku tells Tinubu They warned that awareness campaigns alone would not protect young people from depression, anxiety, substance abuse, suicide risk and the growing psychological pressures associated with social media, insecurity, and other social challenges. The experts, who spoke at the 4th Vanguard mental health summit on Friday in Lagos, stressed that government, health professionals, schools, families, religious institutions, the media and technology platforms must share responsibility for protecting young people’s mental well-being. They urged the Federal Government and state governments to move beyond policy declarations to full implementation of the Mental Health Act, adequate funding of mental health services, integration of care into primary healthcare and the establishment of accessible counselling and referral systems in schools. In his presentation titled: “Making Youth Mental Health Everyone’s Business: From Policy to Practice”, President of the Nigerian Medical Association, (NMA) Prof. Ernest Omoti, represented by the association’s Financial Secretary, and also a professor of psychiatry, Prof. Olayinka Atilola, said youth mental health must become everyone’s business, with practical action replacing isolated interventions. Atilola called for the implementation and funding of the Mental Health Act, the National Mental Health Policy and the National Suicide Prevention Strategic Framework, alongside the integration of mental health services into primary healthcare. Omoti also stressed the need to train a multidisciplinary mental health workforce and establish counselling and referral systems in schools and universities. Families, religious leaders, community organisations and the media, he said, had important roles to play in reducing stigma, identifying distress early and ensuring that young people receive appropriate support. He urged people to listen to young people without rushing to judge them, stressing: “Listen before you label.” The NMA president also called for responsible media reporting of suicide and greater participation of young people in decisions affecting their mental health. Mental Health Act: Experts demand implementation A major concern raised at the summit was the gap between Nigeria’s mental health policies and their implementation. A Professor of Psychiatry, Prof. Taiwo Lateef Sheikh, argued that mental health should be treated as an essential component of national development rather than a marginal health issue. He called for the effective implementation of the Mental Health Act, including measures to decriminalise attempted suicide, expand community-based services and improve access to treatment. Sheikh said the country must recognise the wider social consequences of untreated mental health conditions, particularly the effects of conflict, insecurity, displacement and trauma on individuals, families and communities. He also advocated investment in what he described as “psychological infrastructure”, arguing that the country’s development priorities should extend beyond physical infrastructure to include the emotional and psychological well-being of its people. According to him, restoring mental well-being, trust and social cohesion is important to national progress, while mental health has value beyond its contribution to economic productivity. Speaking, President of the Association of Psychiatric Association of Nigeria, (APN), Dr. Nyamali Veronica Oluyemisi, also called for urgent implementation of the Mental Health Act. She urged the government to establish the department and Mental Health Fund provided for under the law and ensure that mental health services receive dedicated, sustained funding. Nyamali further called on state governments to domesticate and implement relevant provisions of the Act, while integrating mental health services into primary healthcare and community-based care. She advocated the training and deployment of mental health focal persons in secondary and tertiary schools to identify students experiencing psychological distress and link them with appropriate services. The APN president also called for wider access to affordable treatment, the use of telehealth where appropriate, stronger public education and measurable targets against which progress could be assessed before the next summit. Social media, new pressure on young minds The experts also warned that the digital environment had created additional challenges for young people, requiring coordinated action from parents, schools, health professionals, technology platforms and policymakers. Speaking, a professor of Psychiatry, Professor Mashudat Abiola Bello-Mojeed, who spoke on protecting young minds in the age of social media, highlighted concerns around cyberbullying, online exploitation, misinformation, unhealthy social comparison and pressures linked to body image and sleep disruption. She called for stronger national coordination to address online harms and urged schools to establish clear safeguarding policies, reporting channels and counselling support for students affected by cyberbullying. Bello-Mojeed cautioned against relying solely on blanket restrictions, stressing the importance of building trust between parents and young people while equipping children with digital literacy and the ability to recognise harmful online experiences. She also called for greater accountability in the digital environment and urged clinicians to consider young people’s online experiences when assessing their mental health. Her recommendations included the SAFE-MIND framework as part of a broader approach to protecting young people in an increasingly digital world. Drug abuse, mental health-linked Also, the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, NDLEA, Brig. Gen. Mohamed Buba Marwa (retd.), warned that substance abuse and mental health problems frequently reinforce each other, making prevention, treatment and rehabilitation as important as enforcement. Represented by the Assistant Comptroller General, Archie- Abia Ibinabo, said the human distress behind drug abuse must not be ignored in efforts to address the problem. “Behind almost every case of drug abuse is a story of pain: anxiety nobody noticed, depression nobody named, trauma nobody treated,” Marwa said. He urged stakeholders to reach young people with appropriate information, support and treatment before substance use develops into more serious problems. “We must meet young people where they are,” he said. Marwa disclosed that the NDLEA had counselled, treated and rehabilitated 53,843 people through its 31 rehabilitation centres, while its War Against Drug Abuse, WADA, initiative had conducted 17,213 outreach activities in five years. He called for stronger community-based prevention, early intervention in schools, affordable treatment outside major cities and the integration of mental health support into primary healthcare. Marwa also urged stakeholders to challenge the online glamorisation of drugs and reduce the stigma that often prevents people with substance-use and mental health problems from seeking help. He stressed that a comprehensive response must combine law enforcement with prevention, counselling, treatment and rehabilitation. Affordable care, confidentiality essential Also speaking on behalf of the Lagos State Controller of Corrections, Mr. Daramola George, represented by Mr. Ajayi Francis Akinlou, also called for accessible, quality and confidential mental health services. He emphasised the need to strengthen community and primary healthcare services, provide young people with reliable, age-appropriate digital information and protect their privacy when they seek help. It also urged the media to report suicide and self-harm responsibly, while encouraging young people to participate in developing policies and programmes intended to address their needs. He stressed that discussions about mental health must lead to concrete interventions rather than end with expressions of concern. Treatment options and early intervention Also, a UK-based consultant psychiatrist, Dr. Olufemi Oluwatayo highlighted the importance of recognising mental health conditions early and ensuring that young people receive appropriate, evidence-based care. He identified depression, anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder among conditions that may affect young people, noting that treatment should be tailored to the individual and may include psychotherapy, medication or a combination of interventions. Oluwatayo also discussed transcranial magnetic stimulation, TMS, as a possible treatment option for selected patients with depression who have not responded adequately to established treatments. Citing the BRIGhTMIND trial involving 255 patients with treatment-resistant depression, he said the treatment involved 20 sessions over four to six weeks. However, he stressed that TMS should not be presented as a universal solution for mental health conditions. Potential side effects and suitability must be assessed by qualified professionals, and the treatment does not replace established care for every patient. The presentation reinforced calls for improved access to mental health professionals, early assessment and treatment options suited to patients’ needs. From summit declarations to accountability In his welcome remarks, Vanguard Editor, Mr Eze Anaba, challenged participating organisations to ensure that the summit produced practical commitments rather than another round of discussions. He urged each organisation to identify specific actions, assign responsibility to named individuals and set deadlines for delivery, with progress assessed over the following year. The approach, he stressed, would help determine whether the commitments made at the summit translated into tangible improvements. Expert urges treatment over punishment A US based specialist, Dr Daniel Ikpechukwu, said Nigeria must rethink how its justice system handles young people whose involvement with drugs leads to offending, with greater emphasis on addiction treatment, rehabilitation and recovery rather than punishment alone. In his presentation, titled: “Youth Drug Addiction and the Justice System: Advancing Treatment, Rehabilitation and Recovery in Nigeria”, Ikpechukwu, a substance abuse and behavioural health counsellor and adjunct professor of psychology at Georgia Gwinnett College, United States, highlighted the need to balance accountability with appropriate care for young people affected by substance dependence. Nigeria’s national drug use survey estimated that 14.4 per cent of people aged 15 to 64, representing about 14.3 million people, had used psychoactive substances. The scale of the problem calls for coordinated action involving healthcare providers, families, communities, and the justice system. For young people whose substance use is linked to offending, the consequences can extend beyond legal penalties to their health, education, family relationships and employment prospects. Untreated dependence may compound these difficulties and make rehabilitation more challenging. A key priority is early identification and professional assessment to determine the appropriate intervention. Not every young person who uses drugs is dependent, making individual assessment essential. Police officers, prosecutors, judges and correctional personnel also need training to recognise possible substance use disorders and facilitate referrals for treatment. Where legally appropriate, treatment based alternatives may complement conventional justice measures without compromising accountability or public safety. Rehabilitation must continue beyond formal treatment. Follow up care, counselling, family support and opportunities to return to education or employment can help young people sustain recovery and rebuild their lives. Government agencies responsible for health, justice, education and drug control need to coordinate their efforts, expand access to qualified treatment providers and ensure continuity of care. Schools, families and youth organisations also have a role in identifying warning signs and directing young people to professional help early. Sustained funding, trained personnel and accessible treatment facilities are essential. Relevant agencies should also track treatment access, rehabilitation outcomes and continuity of care to determine whether interventions are producing lasting results. However, the call for accountability ran through the discussions, with experts emphasising that government agencies must fund and implement policies, schools must establish support and referral systems, health institutions must expand access to care, families must listen without stigma, and digital platforms must take online harms seriously. For young Nigerians confronting psychological distress, the experts said, the central challenge is not simply whether the country recognises the importance of mental health, but whether help is available when and where it is needed. They insisted that Nigeria must move from awareness to implementation, from policy to funded services, and from promises to measurable action if it is to protect the mental well-being and future of its young people. Vanguard News The post Vanguard summit: Experts demand action on Mental Health Act, school counselling, affordable care appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: PVC collection: Low turnout of registered voters nationwide
items.description: By Dayo Johnson The first day of the collection of Permanent Voters Cards witnessed low turnout of registered voters across the states yesterday as the Independent National Electoral Commission commenced the display of the National Register of Voters and the collection of Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) at the Ward/Registration Area levels. Read Also: 2027: 30 days can’t erase over three years of hardship, Atiku tells Tinubu The commission however said the turnout was relatively low because it was the first day of the exercise and expressed optimism that there would be an improvement with time. While the exercise began smoothly and peacefully in many states, eligible voters in Umuahia, Abia State, expressed anger and disappointment over their inability to collect their PVCs following the absence of INEC officials at some designated collection centres. The exercise followed an announcement by the Commission that PVCs are now ready for collection. INEC had said; “Registered in 2025? Your PVC is now ready for collection. The cards are available for fresh registrants, transfers, replacements, and those who carried out information updates or reviews in 2025. Voters from previous registration exercises can also collect theirs. “If you registered, requested a transfer, or applied for a replacement of a lost or damaged PVC during the first phase, your PVC will be available for collection,” the Commission said. It added that “Uncollected PVCs from previous voter registration exercises will also be available.” Collection at the Registration Areas (RAs) runs from Friday, October 9, to Thursday, October 15, 2026. From Friday, October 16, 2026, it moved to the Local Government Areas LGAs. INEC’s schedule puts the hours at 9am to 3pm. In the same period, the Commission said, “From Friday, 9th to Thursday, 15th October 2026, the Independent National Electoral Commission INEC will display the National Register of Voters for public scrutiny at all Registration Areas nationwide.” FCT At the Government Secondary School in Area 10, Garki, INEC officials were on ground to issue the cards, but the turnout was thin. An official at the centre said the low turnout was probably because it was the first day. She advised members of the public to avoid the late-hour rush by collecting their cards early. Benue In Benue, the exercise began smoothly and peacefully across the state, with INEC expressing optimism that it would continue without hitches. The Public Affairs Officer of INEC in Benue State, Peace Ogoyi, said that the commission had put necessary measures in place to ensure a hitch-free exercise. She said the display of the register to enable voters make claims and objections would continue at the Ward and Registration Area levels until October 15, while PVC collection would take place simultaneously at the same locations. Ogoyi added that PVC collection would continue at the commission’s Local Government Area offices from October 16. Similarly, the Electoral Officer for Makurdi Local Government Area, Mr. Silas Rimdan, said the exercise commenced smoothly and peacefully in the area. Rimdan, however, observed that the turnout on the first day was relatively low, expressing hope that more residents would participate as the exercise progressed. “This is day one, and we have started well. Though, as usual, the turnout is not very impressive, we expect it to increase as the day goes by,” he said. Ogun Vanguard correspondent, who monitored the exercise in Abeokuta, the state capital, observed an impressive turnout of prospective voters at the collection centres. It was also observed that prospective voters presented their voter registration slips or valid means of identification before collecting their cards. Speaking with Vanguard, a prospective voter, Abidemi Adelowo, who visited a collection centre to obtain his PVC, commended INEC for organising the exercise. Adelowo described the process as smooth and hitch-free. Also speaking, Omotara Adeniyi said, there was no challenge in collecting her PVC, commending the INEC for creating awareness. Oyo In Oyo state, INEC confirmed the relatively low turnout recorded on the first day of the exercise but expressed optimism that more registered voters would turn up as the process progressed. The Head of the Publicity Unit of INEC in Oyo State, Olayiwola Awolowo, in an interview with Vanguard said, “being the first day, the turnout is relatively low, but we expect the situation to improve with time. Since the exercise is for seven days, the turnout will improve with time”. Ondo The collection of Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) across Ondo State took off smoothly on Monday, but turnout was considerably low. Prospective voters trickled to centres across Akure, the state capital, on the first day of the exercise. Those interviewed appreciated the electoral umpire for the gesture, saying they had been given the opportunity to exercise their franchise during the coming general elections. In an interview, the spokesperson for the commission in Ondo State, Yinka Ogunseye, confirmed that turnout was “considerably low because it was the first day of the exercise.” Ogunseye said turnout would keep increasing by the day until the last day of the exercise. He urged all eligible persons concerned to take advantage of this opportunity and avoid waiting until rush hours or the last day before visiting their designated registration areas. Ogunseye appealed members of the public to “visit their respective Registration Areas during the seven-day period to participate in the exercise and bring any legitimate claims or objections to the attention of designated INEC officials” Ekiti In Ekiti state, at one of the collection centres in Ado-Ekiti, Omole Olaleye stated that they were informed that the collection would run from 9am to 3pm daily, stressing that the process had been seamless since his arrival. “When I got here, the process was seamless and I thank INEC For that”. Another registered voter, Bose Adedeji said the commission only checked her name on the voter’s register and handed her the card after confirming her identity. Abia Eligible voters in Umuahia, Abia State, on Friday expressed anger and disappointment over their inability to collect their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) on the opening day of nationwide collection, following the absence of Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) officials at some designated collection centres. At Ugba Primary School Umuahia, no INEC staff was sighted at the centre when Vanguard visited around 2pm. Similarly, when our correspondent visited School Road Primary School, Umuahia, at about 2:42 pm, no INEC official was sighted at the centre. Inquiries, however, indicated that the officials who had earlier arrived for the exercise had left. Some prospective voters, who said they had made repeated trips to the centre, accused INEC of frustrating their efforts to obtain their PVCs ahead of the 2027 general elections. One of them, Mr Innocent Odoenelam, a resident of World Bank Housing Estate, Umuahia, said he rushed to the centre after hearing a radio announcement that the cards were ready for collection, only to be told that officials had closed for the day. Odoenelam, who said he arrived at about 2:30 pm, described the experience as discouraging, especially as the official closing time was 3 pm. Odoenelam, however, vowed to return on Monday because he was determined to vote. Another voter, Mr. Francis Egwuibe, said he had visited the centre as early as 8:30 am but left after waiting beyond 9 am without seeing any official. He said he returned in the afternoon, hoping to collect his card, only to discover that the officials had departed. Egwuibe questioned why INEC personnel could not remain at the centre throughout the announced collection period, considering the time and transportation costs incurred by voters. Similarly, a female voter, Chioma Njoku, accused INEC of treating prospective voters as though they had no value, warning that such experiences could discourage people willing to participate in the electoral process. The frustrated voters urged INEC to improve its arrangements and ensure that eligible citizens could obtain their cards without unnecessary hardship. When contacted, INEC spokesperson in Abia, Mr Victor Abraham promised to revert after necessary inquiries but had yet to do so as at the time of filing this report. Ebonyi In Ebonyi State, the Voter Education officer in INEC office Mrs. Esther Idam expressed the commission’s readiness to be in all the wards. She stated that the materials were distributed to various wards from INEC offices in local government areas of the state. Our Correspondent who monitored the exercise in Abakaliki observed that there were INEC officials in some wards visited. But at the time of monitoring of the exercise between 11 am and 2pm there was low turnout, only few people came up to check their names at the displayed registers while nobody came up to collect their PVC at the time. Enugu In Enugu State, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) disclosed that Enugu State has 2, 213,768 registered voters, and eligible voters to collect their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) and participate in the ongoing claims and objections exercise. The Resident Electoral Commissioner (REC) in the state, Dr. Chukwuemeka Chukwu, while briefing journalists on the commencement of the nationwide Display and Hearing of Claims and Objections and PVC collection, urged eligible residents to take advantage of the exercise rather than wait until the last minute. The PVC collection exercise commenced across Enugu State on Friday and was progressing smoothly as of the time of filing this report. Katsina The Independent National Electoral Commission INEC has commenced the distribution of Permanent Voter Cards PVCs across electoral wards in Katsina, urging eligible registrants to collect their cards promptly to ensure their participation in future elections. The Public Relations Officer of INEC in Katsina, Aliyu Abdullahi Garba Adosa disclosed that the exercise covers individuals who registered during the first phase of the Continuous Voter Registration exercise between August and December 2021 as well as those who applied for corrections to their voter details or replacement of lost cards. Adosa said the commission had deployed personnel and distributed the available cards to designated Registration Area Centres across the state’s electoral wards to ensure an orderly and accessible collection process. He added that reports from the centres indicated that a considerable number of eligible voters had turned out on the first day. He observed that turnout in some centres was below expectations, despite the enthusiasm previously demonstrated by residents who had repeatedly asked when their PVCs would be available for collection. According to him, the commission had anticipated a much larger turnout, considering the public interest generated before the exercise commenced. Kwara The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) in Kwara state has dispatched 32,518 Permanent Voters Cards(PVC) under incident and transfer across the sixteen local governments in the state. The spokesman of INEC in the state Ibrahim Abdulkadir told Vanguard that the concerned electorates who had transferred or damaged their PVC are expected to collect the PVC at various wards within one week after which the collection would be transferred to headquarters of the local government. An electorate in Magaji Are ward 2 in Ilorin East local government Farouk Mohammed who spoke with Vanguard said he collected his PVC without any hitch. According to him,” I found my name on the displayed list based on alphabetical order and the INEC officer gave me my PVC,there were no problems at all, I’m ready to cast my vote.” Anambra In Anambra state, the state Resident Electoral Commissioner,REC, Dr Elizabeth Agwu, said that the distribution of PVCs are for those who registered between January and July 2025 before the governorship election of November last year. She called on the local government chairmen to begin an awareness campaign in their areas through town criers to inform the people that collection of PVCs had started. She, however, expressed worry that political parties were not campaigning for the 2027 elections and hoped that they were not planning to scuttle the election. “Start your campaigns and stop tempting our staff with money. Go and do your homework because there’s no longer a shortcut to winning” the REC advised Bayelsa In Bayelsa state, the Independent National Electoral Commission ,INEC, has commenced the distribution of Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) across the eight local government areas of Bayelsa State ahead of the 2027 general elections, with some prospective voters encountering difficulties locating their polling units and retrieving their cards. The state Resident Electoral Commissioner ,REC, Mallam Shaka, who flagged off the exercise on Friday at the commission’s state headquarters in Yenagoa, said the first phase of the distribution covered voters who registered or applied for transfer of their voting locations during the Continuous Voter Registration ,CVR, exercise conducted between August and December 2025. The REC also announced that voters who registered during previous CVR exercises between 2011 and 2022 but had yet to collect their PVCs could visit INEC offices in their respective local government areas between October 9 and 15 to retrieve the cards. However, some prospective voters encountered difficulties, including missing names on the displayed register and challenges identifying their assigned polling units. Some applicants who had lost their PVCs were reportedly asked to return next month because their cases were not covered by the current distribution batch. One of the affected residents, Mr Chidi Timothy, who recently applied for a transfer of his voting location to Yenagoa following his relocation to Bayelsa State on official duty, said he could not collect his card because he was unable to establish the polling unit to which it had been assigned. Timothy said although his name appeared on the register, the inability to identify his polling unit made it difficult for officials to locate his PVC among the cards available for collection. Borno In Borno state, the head of voter education and publicity, Ibrahim Shuaibu said the display and distribution of permanent voters cards will be carried out in phases, while the INEC would continue to give a timeline for claims and objections. He added that exercise would be extended to the Ward level to ensure massive compliance. Shuaibu also expressed satisfaction with the turn out of people to crosscheck and obtain their PVCs. He noted that the ongoing distribution of the PVCs was for those who participated in the registration exercise in August and December last year, while INEC still awaits more PVCs from the Commission’s headquarters. Steve Oko; Peter Duru; Vincent Ujumadu; Rotimi Ojomoyela; Demola Akinyemi; Omeiza Ajayi; Ndahi Marama; Emem Idio; Jeff Agbodo; Chinedu Adonu. & Fauziyya Lawal contributed to this report. items.title: Mobile money : La BCEAO relève le plafond des comptes à 4 millions FCFA et les rechargements mensuels à 15 millions
items.description: À compter du 2 novembre 2026, les usagers de monnaie électronique au sein de l'Union monétaire ouest-africaine (UMOA) bénéficieront d'un assouplissement significatif des plafonds de leurs portefeuilles électroniques. Conformément à l'Instruction n°20 publiée le 8 octobre 2026 par la Banque Centrale des États de l'Afrique de l'Ouest (BCEAO), la limite de détention par client passera de 2 à 4 millions FCFA, tandis que le plafond cumulé de rechargement mensuel atteindra 15 millions FCFA. En contrepartie de cette flexibilité accordée aux utilisateurs, l'institution d'émission impose aux Émetteurs de monnaie électronique (EME) un encadrement renforcé de leurs réserves et des règles de liquidité immédiate afin de garantir la sécurité des fonds déposés. Le cadre réglementaire régissant la monnaie électronique dans l'espace de l'Union monétaire ouest-africaine (UMOA) s'apprête à évoluer. Dans sa décision référencée Instruction n°20, promulguée le 8 octobre 2026, la Banque Centrale des États de l'Afrique de l'Ouest (BCEAO) a apporté des modifications à l'Instruction n°008-05-2015 du 21 mai 2015, texte fondateur encadrant les conditions et modalités d'exercice des émetteurs de monnaie électronique (EME). La mesure phare de cette réforme réside dans la révision des capacités financières autorisées sur les portefeuilles électroniques des usagers. À partir du 2 novembre 2026, un client pourra détenir jusqu'à 4 millions FCFA sur l'ensemble de ses comptes auprès d'un même émetteur, contre une limite fixée à 2 millions FCFA auparavant. Parallèlement, le montant cumulé de ses rechargements mensuels grimpe à 15 millions FCFA, contre 10 millions FCFA dans le dispositif antérieur. Si ces nouveaux seuils offrent une marge de manœuvre élargie aux utilisateurs, toute demande visant à dépasser l'un de ces plafonds devra faire l'objet d'une autorisation préalable délivrée par la Banque Centrale. L'institution d'émission a précisé qu'elle ferait preuve d'une vigilance particulière concernant le suivi des opérations, la gestion des risques et les mesures de contrôle renforcé. Il convient de souligner que les professionnels agissant en qualité de distributeurs ou d'accepteurs de monnaie électronique ne sont pas assujettis à ces restrictions. En vis-à-vis de cette souplesse accordée aux clients, la BCEAO impose un contrôle plus strict sur la conservation de l'argent déposé par le public. Les émetteurs de mobile money ont désormais l'obligation de placer ces fonds exclusivement dans des comptes bancaires, des institutions de microfinance, ou encore dans des titres d'État et d'entreprises cotées en bourse. Pour assurer que les clients puissent procéder au retrait de leurs disponibilités à tout moment, la réglementation exige qu'au moins 65 % des fonds en circulation soient conservés sur des comptes bancaires immédiatement accessibles. De plus, les réserves constituées doivent obligatoirement être comptabilisées à la valeur la plus basse retenue entre leur prix d'achat et leur valeur actuelle sur le marché. Selon les explications fournies par la BCEAO, l'ensemble de ces nouvelles dispositions vise à adapter le dispositif réglementaire du secteur financier pour assurer un meilleur encadrement de la gestion des risques ainsi que de la liquidité des établissements concernés. items.title: Mystère et émotion au secteur 23 de Bobo-Dioulasso : Le « suicide » d’un jeune homme sème le doute secteur N° 23
items.description: Dans la matinée du 4 octobre 2026, les habitants du quartier Kiri, situé au secteur N° 23 de Bobo-Dioulasso, ont fait une macabre découverte en retrouvant le corps sans vie d'un jeune homme d'environ 26 ans, pendu au bout d'une corde. Bien que les premiers témoignages aient évoqué un geste désespéré, la scène suscite un vif trouble et de nombreuses interrogations parmi les riverains. Selon les informations rapportées par le média Libération Burkina , plusieurs détails troublants observés sur place notamment des pieds touchant le sol et une corde ne serrant pas le cou de la victime alimentent la suspicion d'un homicide travesti en suicide. C'est un climat de stupeur et d'incompréhension qui règne au quartier Kiri, dans le secteur N° 23 de Bobo-Dioulasso. Dans la matinée du lundi 4 octobre 2026, la découverte du corps sans vie d'un jeune homme âgé d'environ 26 ans a plongé les résidents dans la consternation. Aussitôt le drame découvert, les habitants se sont rassemblés sur les lieux où la victime apparaissait suspendue au bout d'une corde. Si les premières rumeurs ont rapidement véhiculé l'hypothèse d'un suicide, la vision de la scène a instillé un profond doute au sein de la population locale. D'après les constatations de témoins oculaires relayées par Libération Burkina , la position de la victime remet vivement en cause la thèse d'un acte volontaire. En effet, les personnes présentes ont remarqué que les pieds du jeune homme touchaient directement le sol et que le lien ne lui serrait pas le cou. Ces constatations matérielles ont immédiatement suscité une vague de spéculations et d'inquiétudes parmi les riverains. Pour plusieurs témoins, ces éléments rendent la thèse d'une pendaison autonome particulièrement peu crédible. Une interrogation dérangeante est désormais sur toutes les lèvres à Kiri : la victime a-t-elle été tuée puis suspendue afin de simuler un suicide et égarer les soupçons ? Alors que le mystère reste entier autour des circonstances de ce drame, les habitants du secteur N° 23 attendent désormais que toute la lumière soit faite sur cette tragique affaire. items.title: Tragédie routière sur l’axe Bobo-Dédougou: Un enfant de 12 ans fauché par un véhicule à Satiri, la série noire continue
items.description: Un nouveau drame de la circulation est venu endeuiller le village de Kadomba, dans la commune de Satiri, ce jeudi 8 octobre 2026 aux environs de 11 heures. Selon les informations rapportées par le média Guriko Info , un véhicule tout-terrain en provenance de Dédougou a brusquement quitté la chaussée sur la Route nationale 10 (RN10), percutant un engin à deux roues puis un hangar sous lequel se trouvait un enfant de 12 ans, élève en classe de CM2, qui a perdu la vie. Alors que le conducteur invoque l'éclatement d'un pneu et que des témoins dénoncent une vitesse excessive, cet accident porte à sept le nombre de décès enregistrés sur ce tronçon depuis le début de l'année, d'après les autorités locales. La douleur et la consternation ont une fois de plus envahi la commune rurale de Satiri, située sur l'axe Bobo-Dioulasso–Dédougou. D'après les informations publiées par le média Guriko Info , le paisible village de Kadomba, niché à environ sept kilomètres du chef-lieu de la commune, a été le théâtre d'une collision brutale et mortelle sur la Route nationale 10 (RN10), le jeudi 8 octobre 2026 aux environs de 11 heures. Selon les faits relayés par Guriko Info , un véhicule de type Toyota 4Runner circulait en direction de Bobo-Dioulasso en provenance de Dédougou. Pour des raisons que l'enquête devra préciser, l'automobile a brusquement quitté la voie bitumée. Dans sa trajectoire incontrôlée, l'engin a d'abord percuté un deux-roues avant d'aller s'encastrer violemment sous un hangar. C'est sous cet abri que se trouvait la jeune victime, un enfant de 12 ans, élève en classe de CM2. La violence du choc ne lui a laissé aucune chance : le jeune garçon est décédé sur le coup, plongeant sa famille et l'ensemble de la communauté villageoise dans une profonde affliction. Sur l'origine exacte du drame, les premiers éléments d'explication divergent. Le conducteur de la voiture, qui voyageait seul à bord, a affirmé que l'accident avait été provoqué par l'éclatement soudain d'un pneu. Toutefois, plusieurs témoins présents sur les lieux mettent en cause la conduite de l'automobiliste, évoquant une vitesse excessive inadaptée à la traversée de cette zone habitée. Au-delà de ce drame individuel poignant, cet accident remet en lumière la dangerosité récurrente de la RN10 dans la traversée de la commune de Satiri. D'après les chiffres communiqués par le préfet de Satiri, Emmanuel Ouédraogo, cet évènement constitue le 28ᵉ accident de la circulation répertorié en 2026 sur le tronçon traversant sa circonscription. Cette série noire porte désormais le nombre de victimes mortelles à sept décès depuis le début de l'année. Comme le souligne Guriko Info , ce drame rappelle l'urgence d'une prudence accrue au volant et d'un respect strict du Code de la route pour prévenir de nouvelles pertes de vies humaines. items.title: Passengers groan as flight delays, cancellations worsen
items.description: By Dickson Omobola Domestic air travellers are lamenting frequent flight delays and cancellations across airports in the country, with many expressing frustration over prolonged waiting times and disrupted travel plans. Saturday Vanguard also observed that departure halls at several airports across the country have been crowded in recent times, with many stranded and delayed passengers wearing long faces. A visit to the domestic terminals of the Murtala Muhammed Airport, Lagos, Monday, lent credence to the development, as passengers waited for updates on delayed flights. At the domestic terminal of the Nnamdi Azikiwe Airport, Abuja, Tuesday, the departure hall was crowded, with travellers expressing concern over the frequency of flight disruptions. For instance, one of the passengers, Eze, said his flight had been delayed both on his journey from Lagos to Abuja and on his return trip. He said: “My flight was delayed while I was going to Abuja from Lagos. It was delayed as I am returning. I am stressed, honestly. And I am not alone. Delay announcements are many, about four in two hours today. Terrible.” Another passenger, Jeremiah, whose flight from Warri to Lagos was disrupted, Sunday, said he was forced to spend additional money after the flight was rescheduled to the following day. He said: “I had to part away with another money after my flight scheduled for 5pm on Sunday was shifted to the next day. I needed to be in Lagos by 9am on Monday because I had an important meeting to attend.” Recently, a passenger, Segalink, also took to X, formerly Twitter, to express frustration over a prolonged delay on an Air Peace flight from Asaba to Lagos. He wrote: “Air Peace is interesting. Flight P47863 from Asaba to Lagos which was scheduled to depart at 15:00 on 26/09/2026 (yesterday) kept being rescheduled allegedly due to maintenance and the majority of the passengers slept at the airport in the hope of flying only to be told around 12am that they would fly by 5am this morning. “Unfortunately, that promise wasn’t fulfilled until almost 9am today. These were passengers who bought tickets for a 10am flight originally from Asaba to Lagos. No refreshments or hotel accommodation were provided. Is this how we will continue? These are folks who will not permit you to board if you are 15 minutes late to the counter.” Recall that the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority, NCAA’s, Summary of Domestic Airline Flight Disruptions Operations for August, which showed that domestic airlines collectively recorded 4,801 disruptions out of 7,961 operated flights. Air Peace recorded the highest number of disruptions, with 1,337 delayed or cancelled flights out of 1,864 operated during the month. United Nigeria Airlines delayed or cancelled 951 of its 1,231 operated flights, while Enugu State-owned Enugu Air recorded 586 disruptions out of 878 operated flights. ValueJet disrupted 438 of its 767 operated flights. Akwa Ibom State-owned Ibom Air recorded 257 disruptions out of 560 operated flights, while Arik operated 301 flights, of which 188 were delayed and one was cancelled. However, the airlines faulted the statistics, saying most of the disruptions were caused by factors beyond their control. items.title: FG must address challenges killing Nigerian airlines — Aero Contractors MD, Sanusi
items.description: By Dickson Omobola It was a celebratory mood at Aero Contractors headquarters at the Murtala Muhammed Airport, Lagos, on Monday, as the airline celebrated 67 years of operations. Past and current staff of Aero Contractors were present at the event, which was held at its hangar. After the event, the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Aero Contractors, Capt Ado Sanusi, called on Federal Government to focus on genuine industry reform, among other issues. Background: We believe this administration has done well in infrastructure, but we are telling the administration that policy in the sector must address the specific challenges of the industry. I do understand the peculiar challenges affecting the industry, and if policies are not geared towards addressing those challenges, particularly as the Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, has said that over 100 airlines have died, we should address that. Why are they dying? We should not accept the fact that 10 to 15 airlines die in Nigeria and say it’s normal. There is a particular problem that needs to be addressed, and those are the things I believe an industry-focused and genuine reform will address. What do I mean by industry-focused? It needs careful study and looking at the exact problems that we are facing and addressing them. Let me give you an example. Infrastructure is a very simple thing to take care of because if you have the money, you know what to build, then you will go ahead and build it. For instance, the Coastal Highway. Once you do the study and you have the money, you will build it. However, for an industry that has been here for the past 100 years, I think that was the first time that an airline landed in Kano, and an industry where we had the pride of the nation, Nigeria Airways, was shut down, liquidated and everything. An industry where the fastest-growing airline in Nigeria, in West and Central Africa, and in fact, in Africa, arguably, was allowed to go down. These are specific challenges that the industry faces, and I believe it shouldn’t be allowed to be a thing that the private sector should resolve. After all, when we had the banking crisis, federal government stepped in. We don’t need to have an aviation crisis before federal government should step in. While federal government is doing a lot on infrastructure and policy, there are specific challenges affecting the airlines, the parastatals and the support services that need to be addressed for genuine and sustainable growth. There had been intervention in the aviation industry in the past, especially regarding monetary assistance. Some would describe that intervention as putting money into the system without getting adequate results… I would like to address the first one, where you said there was an intervention in aviation. I don’t think there was any aviation intervention. I don’t think so. I think the intervention that brought the Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria, AMCON, to Aero, Arik and other airlines was made for the banks. The banks were failing because the airlines took loans, and the Federal Government created AMCON to rescue the banks. We were the collateral. It was not a genuine intervention to save the aviation industry. The only intervention I know of was by the former Minister of Finance, Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, who gave a loan to the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria, FAAN, to improve their infrastructure, and the Nigerian Airspace Management Agency, NAMA, I think. When I was MD of NAMA, there was this infrastructure development of all the towers, and that was what they called the Central Project, which was given as an intervention loan, which was paid, I believe, by FAAN. But there was no intervention. If you say money has been paid or has been given to the airlines, it is a no. Aviation did not receive any money as intervention money. The banks did, and they rescued them. At 67, what should we be expecting from the oldest airline in Nigeria? Are you bringing in more aircraft? In your speech also, you called for Aero to be protected and recognised by Federal Government. Those words are pregnant with meaning… We have more routes coming up. We intend to renew our fleet. We also intend to increase our capability list for the MRO, meaning we are buying equipment, we are buying tooling and, very soon, we will be an Embraer centre, where we will repair Embraers. We are also looking at enhancing our training capability. We are opening a new training facility very soon, and we intend to grow it. All that is in the future for us is to be adaptive to the yearnings of our customers, and also to be innovative, and also to ensure that we give our customers, either in the MRO, in the school, or in the airline, a seamless, efficient and reliable service. Most importantly for us is to remain safe, and that is what we are doing. For the pregnancy that you are talking about, and you want me to see whether we can predict the child, it is good to make a prediction, but it is extremely important not to pre-empt, because if we pre-empt, the naysayers will kill it. So, I will leave it as a national treasure, and it should be recognised like that, and also protected. I don’t know when to predict, and somebody will shut it down. On MRO, you have done well in the last nine years. I can see that you have brought in some equipment for the MRO. Can you just put the equipment in Naira? I would say we have invested millions in the equipment and tooling. I don’t think we have to mention how much we have spent to do that. Most importantly, we understand the need to have modern tools, and these tools are modern. Yes, there is a lot of money spent to buy them, but as I said, we are adaptive to the new challenges that we are facing in the MRO. In specific terms, how has the Cape Town Convention, CTC, Practice Directions helped your airline? Honestly, I don’t think it has done anything. That is the truth. I can’t say CTC has helped increase my fleet. CTC is giving comfort to the lessors that when they want to take their planes, they are able to take them. It has been in effect for a long time, just that we bastardised it in Nigeria. You can change the law, but you can’t change the people if the people are still not willing to release the assets of those that we have leased from, and we have not gained the confidence. I prefer to gain the confidence of the lessors than have a very strong CTC. After all, some countries are enjoying a lot of leases without enforcing so much of the Cape Town Convention. Small countries and territories. That is because they have gained the confidence of the lessors. In Aero Contractors, we have gained the confidence of some lessors. That is because we are paying our lease rentals, and when there are things to be talked about, we do so. That is how we can do it as an industry, not relying on CTC, which is just giving a platform. You must work to ensure that, as individual airlines, you gain the confidence of your lessors, and then Nigeria will be enjoying the entire CTC. Some airlines have decided to cut down on unprofitable routes. Are you going to follow the trend? What is the debt situation, and can you give us a timeline for when Aero will disengage from AMCON’s receivership? Globally, airlines are reducing flights or cutting off routes that are not profitable. Aero Contractors is probably going to do the reverse because what we look at is that whenever there is this type of crisis, we see opportunities. This management will look and see opportunities building up. As airlines are withdrawing from a particular sector, we are also looking and choosing the right equipment and the right time and price to make sure that we stay in business. Globally, that’s the trend because of the high cost of Jet A1, but we in Aero Contractors are having a holistic approach to it. We are looking at the crisis as an opportunity for us to grow. As the saying goes, you cannot shrink yourself to greatness. You can’t be cutting routes and you think you will grow. We are very grateful for our relationship with AMCON. They came to Aero Contractors when we needed them the most, and they gave us a second chance. For the timeline, I think that question should go to the receivership and AMCON. I am saddled with the responsibility that the airline keeps running and employing more Nigerians. items.title: Owerri Airport to close for 25 days for runway rehabilitation ahead of Christmas – FG
items.description: Federal Government, in collaboration with the Imo State Government, will temporarily close the Sam Mbakwe International Cargo Airport in Owerri for approximately 25 days starting October 20, 2026, to carry out essential runway repairs and extension works. Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, announced the closure in a press statement, emphasizing that the intervention is critical to ensure aviation safety, increase capacity, and improve operational efficiency ahead of the traditional surge in Christmas travel to the South-East. The rehabilitation project will address deteriorated sections of the runway pavement, treat extensive surface cracks, and fill potholes. Alongside resurfacing, the planned runway extension aims to upgrade the airport’s capacity to accommodate larger, wide-body aircraft, subject to regulatory requirements. The decision follows an agreement between the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN), Imo State Governor Senator Hope Uzodinma, and other regional stakeholders. Keyamo praised the partnership between the federal and state governments, noting that a modernized airport will serve as a critical gateway for businesses and support the economic development of the region. Addressing the inevitable disruptions, the Ministry acknowledged the inconvenience the closure will cause to airport users but stressed that aviation safety cannot be compromised. The temporary shutdown is necessary to allow contractors unhindered access to effectively execute the upgrades. Passengers scheduled to travel through Owerri during the 25-day closure period are advised to contact their respective airlines immediately to arrange for flight cancellations, rescheduling, or alternative travel plans. The government has pledged to continue engaging with airlines and stakeholders to minimize disruptions, with confirmed reopening dates to be communicated through official channels. items.title: NAFDAC finds toxic pesticides in beans, seizes N800m banned chemical
items.description: By Chioma Obinna The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, (NAFDAC), yesterday warned that the continued circulation and misuse of banned pesticides in Nigeria pose serious threats to public health, raising concerns over the detection of pesticide residues above permitted safety limits in some samples of beans. The agency disclosed that it had seized banned agrochemicals worth more than ₦800 million in Ogun, Ondo, Osun and Oyo states in 2025, while a separate operation in Kebbi State led to the interception of 67,428 litres of paraquat, a prohibited pesticide, alongside banned atrazine products. NAFDAC also revealed that a recent market study detected residues of pyrethroids and dimethoate above permitted safety limits in some bean samples, underscoring concerns about the use of agricultural chemicals to preserve harvested produce. The Director-General of NAFDAC, Prof. Mojisola Adeyeye, who raised the alarm at a media briefing on pesticide use in agricultural produce in Lagos, said the agency was intensifying surveillance, enforcement and public education to rid the Nigerian market of banned, unregistered, falsified and improperly used pesticides. “NAFDAC is not against the responsible use of pesticides. Rather, the agency seeks to ensure that pesticides sold or used in Nigeria are safe, approved and compliant with regulatory requirements,” Adeyeye said. She warned that although pesticides were important for crop protection and agricultural production, improper application, excessive use and failure to observe prescribed waiting periods before harvesting could expose farmers, consumers and the environment to harmful chemicals. “Improper pesticide use can cause serious health problems, including death. Some effects may not appear immediately but can develop gradually over time,” she said. Adeyeye explained that the agency’s concern extended beyond the illegal importation and sale of prohibited chemicals to the misuse of approved pesticides, which could leave dangerous residues on food consumed by Nigerians. The NAFDAC boss said the recent market study on beans revealed residues of pyrethroids and dimethoate exceeding applicable safety limits in some samples. She explained that dimethoate was not approved for preserving harvested beans against pests such as weevils, stressing that chemicals approved for use on crops in the field could not automatically be used for post-harvest preservation. While certain pyrethroids were permitted for post-harvest storage under approved conditions, Adeyeye said users must observe the prescribed withholding period before the produce was consumed. She identified common pesticide misuse practices as applying chemicals in quantities above recommended levels, using products on crops or against pests for which they were not approved, harvesting before the required pre-harvest interval and mixing products improperly. Other dangerous practices, she said, included storing pesticides alongside food, animal feed or household items, reusing empty pesticide containers for domestic purposes and improperly disposing of chemical residues and containers. “Food safety begins on the farm,” Adeyeye said, urging farmers to purchase approved products, follow label instructions, apply recommended quantities and observe all safety precautions. She said protecting Nigerians from harmful pesticide residues required responsible practices across the agricultural value chain, from manufacturers and importers to distributors, agro-input dealers and farmers. Giving details of the agency’s enforcement operations, Adeyeye said NAFDAC seized banned agrochemicals worth more than N800 million in Ogun, Ondo, Osun and Oyo states in 2025. Between September 2024 and July 2026, enforcement operations in the North-West Zone resulted in the seizure, interception or recovery of 2,974 cartons of pesticides containing paraquat, with an estimated value of N148.7 million. Another 120 cartons of pesticides containing chlorpyrifos, valued at more than N17 million, were intercepted during the same period. In a separate operation in Kebbi State, the agency intercepted 5,619 cartons containing 67,428 litres of paraquat and 500 cartons of atrazine products. NAFDAC also sealed four unauthorised pesticide and agrochemical manufacturing facilities in Bichi, Kano State, in July 2026, where officers reportedly discovered unlabelled products, bulk chemicals and packaging materials linked to illicit production. Adeyeye said suspects had been arrested in connection with enforcement operations, with one case undergoing prosecution. She attributed the continued circulation of prohibited pesticides partly to illegal importation and movement across Nigeria’s borders, noting that products banned in the country could enter through neighbouring countries and unauthorised supply channels. “These interceptions after the effective date of the ban indicate that the challenge extends beyond residual stocks to illegal importation, unauthorised local production and distribution,” she saiid. Adeyeye disclosed that the phase-out periods for pesticides containing paraquat, chlorpyrifos and atrazine ended on January 1, 2026. She said the chemicals could no longer legally be manufactured, imported, distributed, sold or used in Nigeria under the agency’s completed regulatory measures. According to her, NAFDAC reviewed registered pesticide active ingredients in 2022 using scientific evidence, its Automated Product Administration and Monitoring System database, and input from relevant experts and stakeholders. The review considered risks to human health and the environment, applicable national regulations and international requirements. Adeyeye also disclosed that NAFDAC had restricted the 100ml pack size of dichlorvos, prohibiting its importation, manufacture and open-market or supermarket sale following concerns about misuse on agricultural produce and its use in suicide. Other permitted pack sizes, she said, remained subject to applicable regulatory controls. The Director-General said the agency was strengthening collaboration with government institutions and law enforcement authorities to identify, seize and remove illegal pesticides from circulation and prosecute offenders where applicable. “No business interest or desire for profit will justify the illegal importation, distribution or sale of banned or non-compliant pesticides,” she said. To reduce the risks associated with improper pesticide use, Adeyeye said NAFDAC had trained more than 2,000 agro-input dealers on the responsible handling and application of agricultural chemicals. She said the agency was also expanding its investigation and enforcement zonal offices from three to six to improve regulatory coverage across the country. Other measures include registration and scientific assessment of pesticide products before market entry, inspection of manufacturing and storage facilities, border checks, market surveillance, laboratory testing and enforcement against businesses involved in illegal production and distribution. Adeyeye added that NAFDAC provided free interim testing for export products to encourage compliance with applicable safety standards and prevent consignments from being rejected in destination countries because of pesticide residues or other regulatory violations. She urged manufacturers and importers to ensure that their products met regulatory requirements, while distributors and agro-input dealers were advised to obtain pesticides only through legitimate channels. Farmers were also urged to buy from recognised agro-input dealers, read and follow product labels, use only recommended quantities and observe prescribed waiting periods before harvesting. Deputy Director of Veterinary Medicine and Allied Products at NAFDAC, Dr. Idayat Mudshiru, said sustained engagement with farmers and other stakeholders remained critical to preventing pesticide misuse. “NAFDAC continues to engage farmers and relevant stakeholders on the responsible use and application of pesticide products,” Mudshiru said. She said the agency was working with industry stakeholders, including CropLife, to strengthen public awareness and promote safe pesticide handling and application. “The advocacy and education efforts are ongoing,” she said, emphasising the need for continued collaboration to protect consumers and the environment. NAFDAC said it would sustain enforcement, public education and stakeholder engagement to ensure that agricultural chemicals were used in accordance with safety requirements and that food reaching Nigerian households met applicable standards. items.title: Des armes de fabrication émiratie pour renforcer les capacités de combat des Forces Royales Air
items.description: Le système THUNDER P-31 figure parmi les solutions de défense avancées développées localement par Halcon, filiale du groupe émirati EDGE. Il s’agit d’un kit de guidage de précision à courte portée conçu pour être installé sur des bombes conventionnelles, leur conférant des capacités de frappe intelligentes et performantes. Le système pèse au total 140 kg, dont 110 kg pour la charge militaire. Le système DESERT STING 16, ou « Dard du désert », est quant à lui une munition planante guidée de haute précision, caractérisée par une conception légère et efficace. Il peut être lancé depuis différentes plateformes, notamment des drones. Son poids total est de 23 kg, avec une charge militaire de 12 kg. Pour suivre ses cibles, cette munition s’appuie sur des technologies de guidage avancées combinant un système de navigation inertielle assisté par satellite (GNSS/INS) et un autodirecteur laser semi-actif (SAL), afin d’assurer une grande précision lors de l’impact. Par ailleurs, le groupe émirati a signé, vendredi, un mémorandum d’entente avec l’Administration de la défense nationale marocaine, en marge du Salon international de l’aéronautique et du spatial de Marrakech. Cet accord vise à définir un cadre permettant d’explorer les possibilités de production locale au Maroc dans les domaines des armes légères à hautes performances et des moteurs aéronautiques, en coopération avec des entreprises marocaines. Dans un communiqué distinct, EDGE a indiqué que cet accord traduit son engagement à répondre aux besoins de ses clients à travers des partenariats régionaux efficaces. Le groupe entend notamment rapprocher les capacités de fabrication des clients, renforcer les chaînes d’approvisionnement et les services de soutien tout au long du cycle de vie des systèmes, ainsi que contribuer au développement de filières industrielles nationales souveraines. Hamad Al Marar, directeur général et président-directeur général du groupe émirati, a déclaré que « le Royaume du Maroc représente un partenaire important pour EDGE en Afrique ». « Ce mémorandum d’entente reflète notre approche fondée sur le partenariat comme socle de la coopération. Notre modèle repose sur le partage des connaissances, la localisation de la production et le transfert de technologie, afin de construire des partenariats mutuellement bénéfiques et de soutenir la croissance de l’industrie nationale, tout en élargissant nos activités » , a-t-il ajouté. Le responsable a également souligné que la coopération avec des entreprises marocaines en vue de localiser la production d’armes à feu éprouvées sur le terrain et de moteurs aéronautiques avancés vise à soutenir la constitution d’une base industrielle capable de répondre aux besoins de défense du Royaume. items.title: INEC begins voters’ register display, PVC distribution in Yobe
items.description: By Maryam Abdul-aziz Usman The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has commenced the display of the preliminary voters’ register and distribution of Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) across the 17 local government areas of Yobe State, giving registered voters seven days to verify their details and report errors. The exercise began at about 9am on Friday, October 9, in line with a directive from the commission’s national headquarters. The Head of Voter Education and Publicity at INEC in Yobe, Nuhu Ibrahim, said the state received its PVCs early, enabling voters to begin collecting their cards before the commencement of the current display exercise. “Yobe is one of the states that received their cards earliest, and voters have been collecting their cards since then. The display officially commenced today and will last for seven days to enable registered voters to identify errors in their details, such as spelling mistakes and incorrect ages, so that the commission can address them promptly,” Ibrahim said. He explained that the current exercise covered the first phase of the registration process, adding that the lists for voters registered during the second and third phases would be displayed later. A visit to Central Primary School in Damaturu Local Government Area showed INEC officials displaying preliminary lists as residents checked their names and sought to collect available PVCs. The Damaturu Local Government Electoral Officer, Ahmed Alhaji Waziri, identified the failure of some voters to present their temporary voter cards and inadequate mobilisation as challenges affecting the exercise. Waziri said temporary voter cards could help officials trace the corresponding PVCs, adding that some applicants who registered during the second and third phases of the Continuous Voter Registration exercise had turned up expecting to collect their cards. He explained that the available PVCs comprised uncollected cards from the 2023 general election and cards produced during the first phase of the latest registration exercise, conducted between August and December 2025. At the ward level, Electoral Officer Alhaji Ibrahim Ibrahim said residents began visiting the centres within hours of the preliminary lists being displayed. “Just a few hours after we displayed the preliminary lists of registered voters, people had already started coming forward to check their names and claim their cards,” he said. One of the voters, Musa Gambo, said he had found his name on the list and intended to collect his PVC. “I have seen my name on the list, and I will collect my Permanent Voter Card,” Gambo said. INEC urged political parties, community leaders and other stakeholders to sustain voter mobilisation, stressing that efforts to encourage eligible citizens to register should be matched with initiatives to ensure they collect their PVCs and participate in the electoral process. The seven-day display also provides registered voters an opportunity to identify errors in their personal details and request corrections by the commission. items.title: Petrol hits N1,900/litre as depot prices surge despite NNPC cut
items.description: •NIPCO raises petrol price by N170 in Port Harcourt; Rain Oil, Matrix hike diesel to N1,900 in Warri; NNPC sells at N1,360, MRS at N1,338 in Lagos; Brent rises to $104.50 per barrel By Udeme Akpan, Energy Editor There are indications that domestic petroleum product prices could rise further as petrol depot prices surged across Lagos, Port Harcourt, Warri and Calabar on Friday, with several marketers in Port Harcourt raising their prices to N1,900 per litre, despite lower pump prices at some filling stations in Lagos. Read Also: 2027: 30 days can’t erase over three years of hardship, Atiku tells Tinubu NIPCO led the increases in Port Harcourt, raising its Premium Motor Spirit, PMS, price by N170 per litre to N1,900 from N1,730, while six other depots increased their prices by N150 to the same level. The developments coincided with an increase in international crude oil prices, as Brent crude climbed to $104.50 per barrel from $104.28, while the US benchmark, West Texas Intermediate, WTI, rose to $91.73 from $91.49. A review of depot prices showed that African Terminal, Ascon, Eterna, Gulf Treasure, Ibachem and Ibeto raised their petrol prices in Port Harcourt to N1,900 per litre from N1,750 each. Duport and Integrated, however, increased their prices to N1,806 per litre from N1,750, representing an increase of N56 per litre. In Lagos, Masters raised its petrol price to N1,350 per litre from N1,303, while Matrix increased its price to N1,360 from N1,330. Sigmund and T.S.L raised their prices to N1,350 per litre from N1,300 each, while NIPCO increased its price to N1,350 from N1,326. In Calabar, Matrix raised its price to N1,370 per litre from N1,315. In Warri, Keonamex, Matrix, Nepal and Parker increased their prices to N1,360 per litre from N1,315 each, while Optima raised its price to N1,360 from N1,330. Pump prices vary At the retail end, the NNPC Limited sold petrol at N1,360 per litre at its filling stations in Lagos and surrounding areas. MRS Oil Nigeria Plc sold the product at N1,338 per litre, while 11 Plc sold at N1,338.80. Independent marketers charged between N1,368 and N1,400 per litre, depending on location. Consequently, motorists patronising MRS and 11 Plc paid less than those buying from some independent marketers, whose prices reached N1,400 per litre. The price differences highlight the divergent pricing trends across the supply chain, with depot prices rising in several locations even as some filling stations continued to sell below the rates charged by independent marketers. Diesel prices climb The diesel market also recorded significant increases in Warri, where Rain Oil and Matrix raised their Automotive Gas Oil, AGO, prices by N180 per litre to N1,900 from N1,720 each. In Port Harcourt, Dangote increased its diesel price to N1,720 per litre from N1,702, while Masters raised its price to N1,825 from N1,788. The increases could add to operating costs for manufacturers, transport operators and other businesses that rely on diesel for power generation and transportation, particularly if the higher prices persist. Crude oil market mixed On the international market, the OPEC Basket rose to $109.50 per barrel from $108.59, while WTI Midland increased to $92.74 from $92.32. Natural gas prices climbed to $3.235 from $3.168, but Murban crude fell to $108.50 per barrel from $110.49. Among refined products, gasoline declined to $3.293 from $3.316, while heating oil dropped to $4.724 from $4.883. The Indian Basket rose to $121.10 per barrel from $117.63. The mixed movements across international benchmarks indicate that domestic depot price increases should not be attributed solely to the day’s crude oil gains. Product replacement costs, supply conditions, transportation expenses and individual marketers’ pricing decisions may also influence local prices. Commenting on the developments in an interview with Vanguard, the Chief Executive Officer of Petroleumprice.ng, Olatide Jeremiah, said: “Despite domestic issues and development in Nigeria, the downstream sector would continue to respond or react to developments at the global oil market.” With petrol reaching N1,900 per litre at several Port Harcourt depots and diesel hitting the same level in Warri, the latest price movements underscore the pressures facing Nigeria’s downstream market and the continuing differences between wholesale and retail prices. items.title: Ghana housing finance conference adopts communiqué to improve affordable housing access
items.description: The National Conference on Housing Finance 2026 has adopted a communiqué committing government, financial institutions, housing developers, labour organisations and other stakeholders to coordinated action to improve access to affordable housing in Ghana. The communiqué, adopted at the Mövenpick Ambassador Hotel in Accra on Thursday, October 8, outlines measures to address barriers to housing finance, promote affordable housing delivery and advance the goal of “Adequate Housing for All.” The conference was convened by the National Housing Fund (NHF) in collaboration with public and private sector stakeholders, bringing together representatives of government, regulators, development partners, employers, academia and civil society. Under the agreement, the NHF has been tasked with coordinating implementation of the commitments and monitoring progress. The NHF pledged to promote innovation in the housing finance sector and expand access to financing for prospective homeowners and housing developers. It committed to developing risk-sharing, guarantee, and other mechanisms to reduce financing barriers, as well as promoting affordable housing finance products for workers in both the formal and informal sectors. The fund also plans to lead the establishment of a national homebuyers database and digital marketplace to connect housing demand with available homes and finance providers. Other commitments include mobilising private investment, supporting social housing for vulnerable and underserved groups, and establishing mechanisms to monitor and report on progress. Workers and labour organisations pledged to promote responsible savings and financial planning to support homeownership. They also committed to participating in housing finance programmes and advocating for solutions that reflect the circumstances of workers in both formal and informal employment. The groups said they would collaborate with government, the Ghana Real Estate Developers Association (GREDA), the NHF and financial institutions to develop sustainable pathways to affordable housing. They further pledged to advocate for inclusive housing policies to ensure workers are not excluded from homeownership opportunities. GREDA committed to promoting the use of appropriate local building materials and improving efficiency in housing delivery to help reduce construction costs and house prices. The association also pledged to encourage green and climate-resilient building practices and collaborate with government, the NHF, financial institutions, workers and employers to develop affordable housing schemes. The communiqué emphasises that improving access to adequate housing will require coordinated action on financing, land administration, urban planning, infrastructure, affordability, sustainability and institutional effectiveness. It also calls for the commitments to be translated into measurable actions, with progress reviewed periodically and dialogue sustained among stakeholders. “The Conference further commits to translating these resolutions into measurable actions, tracking progress periodically and sustaining dialogue among stakeholders to build an accessible, affordable, sustainable and inclusive housing finance system for Ghana,” the communiqué stated. Ghana’s housing deficit has been estimated at more than 1.8 million units, while rapid urbanisation and rising construction costs continue to complicate efforts to provide affordable homes. Access to housing finance remains a significant challenge, particularly for informal sector workers, many of whom may not have the regular income documentation or conventional employment arrangements required by traditional mortgage providers. The conference sought to bring stakeholders across the housing sector together to identify coordinated responses to these challenges. The NHF is expected to lead efforts to implement the agreed commitments and track progress towards the conference’s goal of adequate housing for all.
